lesson.title: Enough Is Enough: Repression and the Trp Operon
lesson.summary: The trp operon is a repressible operon that stays on by default, making the enzymes needed to build tryptophan, and switches off only when tryptophan is already abundant.
lesson.body:
The trp operon in Escherichia coli contains five structural genes, trpE, trpD, trpC, trpB, and trpA, which together encode the enzymes needed to synthesize the amino acid tryptophan from an earlier metabolic precursor. Unlike the lac operon, which is normally off and switched on by its substrate, the trp operon is normally on and is switched off when its end product, tryptophan, becomes abundant. This makes it a repressible operon, the opposite logical arrangement from an inducible one, though it still relies on the same basic tool of negative control, a repressor protein that binds an operator.

A separate gene, trpR, encodes the Trp repressor protein, but on its own this repressor cannot bind the operator; in this inactive form it is sometimes called an aporepressor. When tryptophan is scarce inside the cell, the repressor stays in this inactive form, the operator remains free, and RNA polymerase transcribes trpE through trpA freely, so the cell keeps making the enzymes it needs to build its own tryptophan supply.

When tryptophan is abundant, tryptophan molecules themselves bind directly to the Trp repressor protein, acting as a corepressor. This binding changes the repressor's shape into its active form, which can now bind the operator and block RNA polymerase. With plenty of tryptophan already available, the cell has no need to keep making more of the enzymes that synthesize it, and transcription of the operon shuts down. This is the defining logic of a repressible system: the pathway's own end product is what triggers the repressor and switches the pathway off, rather than a substrate switching it on.

The trp operon also carries a faster, secondary layer of control called attenuation, which fine tunes transcription after it has already started. A short leader sequence just ahead of trpE contains two consecutive codons for tryptophan, and a ribosome translating this leader region stalls at those codons whenever tryptophan, and the charged tRNA that delivers it, is in short supply. That stalling favors the formation of an RNA structure that allows RNA polymerase to keep transcribing into the structural genes. When tryptophan is abundant, the ribosome moves through the leader without stalling, and a different RNA structure forms instead that causes RNA polymerase to stop before it ever reaches the structural genes. Attenuation and repression work on different timescales but push in the same direction, reducing transcription whenever tryptophan is already plentiful.

The trp operon's repression is a useful complement to feedback inhibition, a mechanism where a pathway's end product directly inhibits the activity of an enzyme already made, usually the first enzyme in the pathway, without needing any change in gene expression at all. Feedback inhibition is fast and immediately reversible, adjusting how active existing enzyme molecules are from one moment to the next, while trp operon repression acts more slowly, at the level of whether new enzyme molecules get made in the first place. Together, the two mechanisms let the cell fine tune tryptophan production on two different timescales, an immediate one at the level of enzyme activity, and a slower one at the level of gene expression.
